cards.s: System design
cards.html:
Chapter 9 · Career: The Senior Toolkit. You can now build and operate the pipeline. This chapter is about the other half of a senior role: designing delivery for more than one team, answering interview questions with trade-offs instead of features, and turning two repositories into evidence that a hiring manager believes.

After this level you can:

  • Recognise what makes an answer sound senior, and rewrite junior answers.
  • Work through a system-design question: a delivery platform for ten ML teams.
  • Answer fifteen senior CI/CD questions, and tell honest "tell me about a time" stories from your own project.
  • Turn credit-api and rag-api into a portfolio: README, ADRs, measurements, demo, CV bullets.

cards.s: System design
cards.html: What you build: An interview kit you have rehearsed aloud, a portfolio README with measured numbers, three or more ADRs, and four CV bullets you can defend in any follow-up question.

cards.s: What "senior" sounds like
cards.html:
Interviewers for senior roles rarely ask "what is a pipeline?". They ask open questions and listen for signals. The same knowledge can sound junior or senior:

SignalJunior answerSenior answer
Trade-offs"We used canary deployments.""Canary needs enough traffic for the metrics to mean something; at 50 requests a minute I used a smoke test plus a distribution check instead."
Numbers"The gate prevents bad models.""The split alone moves AUC by ±0.025, so I set the tolerance to 0.03 and fixed the split."
Failure"It worked well.""My first role design let any branch reach production through staging; a review found it, and I split the role."
Scope"I built the pipeline.""I'd turn it into a template so the next team gets it in a day; here is what they may change."
UncertaintyGuesses a fact."I haven't run that at scale; I'd check X and measure Y first."
UsersTalks about tools.Talks about who is affected: the applicant, the reviewer at 2 a.m., the auditor.

cards.s: What "senior" sounds like
cards.html: A useful habit: answer in the order context → options → decision → cost → what I'd watch. "It depends" is a senior phrase only if you then say on what.

cards.s: System design: a delivery platform for ten ML teams
cards.html:
Concept: The question

"You join as a senior ML engineer. Ten teams each build models and deploy them their own way: copied workflows, long-lived AWS keys, manual deploys on Fridays. Design how they should build, test and deliver models. You have 45 minutes."

cards.s: System design: a delivery platform for ten ML teams
cards.html:
Ask before you draw. Each answer changes the design:

  • Online or batch? APIs with latency targets, or nightly scoring jobs, or both. (Both, usually.)
  • How regulated? A bank (four-eyes principle, audit trail, DORA) or a startup?
  • Where do they run today? One AWS account or many; Kubernetes or ECS; how mature is the platform team?
  • What hurts most? Incidents, slow delivery, cost, audit findings? The answer sets your first milestone.
  • How many people for the platform? Two engineers design differently from twenty.

Assume for this answer: a German bank, online and batch models, AWS, ECS today, two platform engineers, and an audit finding about manual production changes.

cards.s: System design: a delivery platform for ten ML teams
System design: a delivery platform for ten ML teams
cards.html:
Walk through it in layers, and give each decision its reason:

  1. Golden-path template. A template repository ("new model service") creates repo, CI, deploy, runbook skeleton, dashboards and a model card in one step (a cookiecutter template, or Backstage software templates if the company runs Backstage). Teams start on the paved road instead of copying last year's workflow.
  2. Reusable workflows, versioned. The steps live once, in a platform repository, released by tag (@v3). Teams call them with a few inputs. Dependabot opens upgrade PRs; each team's CI proves the upgrade. A security fix becomes one release, not ten PRs.

cards.s: System design: a delivery platform for ten ML teams
cards.html:
1. Accounts and identity. Separate AWS accounts for dev, staging and production (AWS Organizations). No long-lived keys: OIDC roles per environment and team; production roles trust only the production environment and, via job_workflow_ref, only the platform's deploy workflow. This removes the audit finding at the root.
  2. Guardrails, not gatekeepers. Organisation rulesets require the platform's check (ci-ok) and reviews on every repo; actions are pinned by SHA; images are scanned, get an SBOM, are signed by digest and verified before production deploys. Teams cannot skip these; everything else is theirs to change.

cards.s: System design: a delivery platform for ten ML teams
cards.html:
1. ML specifics. A shared MLflow registry and artefact store; promotion through gated aliases; a model card and lineage record are required artefacts of every production deploy. Data contracts and metric gates are in the template, thresholds owned by each team.
  2. Release and operations. Continuous delivery with approval for models making credit decisions; canary or blue-green for services with enough traffic; standard JSON logs, an SLO per service, runbook and postmortem templates.
  3. Cost. Mandatory cost tags (team, service, env) enforced in IaC; a monthly cost report per team; budgets per account.

cards.s: System design: a delivery platform for ten ML teams
cards.html:
A platform nobody adopts has failed. Say how you would roll out:

  • Phase 1 (month 1–2): OIDC and the reusable CI workflow with two pilot teams, picked because they have the most pain. Remove their long-lived keys.
  • Phase 2 (month 3–4): deploy workflow, environments, signing; the production account accepts only platform-built images.
  • Phase 3: template for new services; migrate the rest team by team, with office hours, not a deadline email.
  • Measure: DORA measures per team (lead time, deployment frequency, change failure rate, recovery time), share of repos on the current workflow version, number of long-lived keys (target: zero), audit findings closed.

cards.s: System design: a delivery platform for ten ML teams
cards.html:
• Too rigid: teams fork the workflow and drift. Mitigation: inputs for the common variations, an "escape hatch" process, and a platform roadmap teams can influence.
  • Platform team becomes a bottleneck: self-service over tickets; documented contribution path for teams.
  • Big-bang migration: never. Pilot, measure, then expand.

Interview tip

"I'd treat the platform as a product with internal customers: start with the two teams that hurt most, remove long-lived keys first because that's also the audit finding, and measure adoption and lead time, not the number of features we ship."

cards.s: System design: a delivery platform for ten ML teams
cards.html:
Concept: Prompt A: "Design CI/CD for an LLM feature where prompts change weekly."

Key insight: a prompt is code and configuration; it changes model behaviour without a model change. Answer outline: prompts versioned in Git (not in a database UI) and reviewed like code; a golden set with deterministic checks (retrieval hit rate, format, refusal on out-of-scope) as the hard PR gate; LLM-judged quality on a sample as an advisory PR comment and a hard gate nightly; cost caps and a cache keyed on every request parameter; prompt version in every log line; rollout behind a feature flag to a share of users, with user feedback and judge scores compared per prompt version; held-out set to avoid tuning to the golden set. Mention the model provider as a dependency: pin the model version, and treat a model upgrade like a dependency upgrade with the full evaluation.

cards.s: System design: a delivery platform for ten ML teams
cards.html:
Concept: Prompt B: "Nightly batch scoring of 50 million rows."

Key insight: no latency SLO, but a deadline and a correctness SLO (results complete and plausible by 06:00). Answer outline: the scoring job is a versioned container image from the same pipeline, run by a scheduler (Airflow, Step Functions, or a managed batch service) with partitioned input; CI runs the job on a small fixed sample and compares the output distribution with the previous version; before publishing, checks on row counts, null shares and the score distribution against yesterday, with publication blocked if they fail (the batch equivalent of our distribution check); outputs written to a dated location and switched atomically, so rollback is pointing consumers back to yesterday's run; cost by using spot capacity for a retryable job.

cards.s: Explaining your pipeline in an interview
cards.html:
A feature list ("ruff, mypy, pytest, Docker, ECR, ECS, MLflow…") sounds like a tutorial. Interviewers for senior roles listen for decisions: what problem, which options, why this one, what it cost, what broke. Structure the two minutes that way:

Interview tip: A two-minute script: problem, three decisions, what broke

"I built a credit-risk API as a portfolio project, and treated the delivery pipeline as the actual product. The problem: a model can be correct code and still be worse than the one in production, so ordinary CI is not enough.

cards.s: Explaining your pipeline in an interview
cards.html:
Decision one: the pipeline validates data and trains on every PR, and a gate fails the build if ROC-AUC falls below a floor or drops more than 0.03 against the baseline. I chose that tolerance from measurement, not by feel: I retrained twenty times and found that the train/test split alone moves AUC by about ±0.025, so I fixed the split as part of the contract.

Decision two: continuous delivery, not deployment. Every merge goes to staging automatically, with a smoke test and a check that the share of rejected applicants is plausible; production needs an approval. For a credit model, a wrong release is expensive and outcomes arrive months later, so the human gate is worth the delay.

cards.s: Explaining your pipeline in an interview
cards.html:
Decision three: no stored cloud credentials. GitHub Actions gets short-lived AWS credentials through OIDC, with one role per stage. My first version had a single broad role, and a review showed that any branch could have reached production through the staging environment, so I split it and restricted every environment to main.

What I would do next at scale: a shared model registry so that promotion, not retraining, decides what ships; Terraform instead of my shell script; and separate AWS accounts per environment."

cards.s: Explaining your pipeline in an interview
cards.html: Why this works: every paragraph contains a trade-off and a number, it admits a mistake and shows how it was found, and it ends with what you would change, which invites the follow-up questions you have prepared. Never say "we" for a solo project, and do not claim production traffic you did not have; "in my project I measured…" is stronger than an invented team result. Chapter 9 has the full interview kit: fifteen senior questions with model answers, and how to turn the what-ifs in this book into honest "tell me about a time" stories.

cards.s: Explaining your pipeline in an interview
cards.html:
Likely follow-up questions, and short answers:

QuestionAnswer in one breath
Why not deploy automatically to production?It depends on reversibility and how fast you learn about mistakes. Credit decisions are costly to reverse and labels arrive months later, so I keep a human approval; with fast labels, canaries and good monitoring I would move to continuous deployment.
How do you avoid flaky metric gates?Measure the variance first, fix seeds and the split, set the tolerance from the measurement, and change the baseline only through a reviewed PR.
How does the champion reach production?In my default setup it does not: deploy trains from the merged commit. With a shared registry, the build exports @champion instead; /health reports code SHA, model version and data hash either way.
How would this scale to big data?Train on samples in PRs, full training as a separate pipeline (SageMaker, Kubeflow or Airflow), data versioned with DVC; CI only orchestrates and gates.

cards.s: Explaining your pipeline in an interview
cards.html:
QuestionAnswer in one breath
What if the new model is bad in production?Smoke test and canary catch crashes; the distribution check catches implausible decisions; for quality, monitoring compares prediction distributions; rollback is redeploying the previous image by SHA, which also restores the old model.

Exercise: Break the data

Change one age value in data/german_credit.csv to 150 and push a branch. Which job fails first, with which message? Revert.

Exercise: Make retrieval worse

cards.s: Explaining your pipeline in an interview
cards.html:
In rag-api, change chunk_markdown to put the whole document into one chunk, run eval/run_eval.py, and explain the change in MRR. Then run with --k 1 (add a hit_rate_at_1 threshold to eval/thresholds.json first) and compare.

Exercise: Paired promotion

Rewrite promote.py so that it loads both @champion and the new version, scores both on the same current test split, and promotes only if the challenger passes the gate against the champion's score on those rows. Test it locally with the SQLite tracking URI.

Exercise: A slice gate

cards.s: Explaining your pipeline in an interview
cards.html:
Extend train.py to also report roc_auc_age_lt_25, add a floor of 0.65 for it in thresholds.json, and make sure gate.check() handles it without code changes. What happens if a sample contains fewer than two classes in the slice?

Exercise: Fix the cache key

Change the cache key in rag_api/llm.py so that it includes every request parameter, make max_tokens a constructor argument, and add a unit test that proves two different max_tokens values produce two different cache files.

Checkpoint: you should now be able to…

cards.s: Explaining your pipeline in an interview
cards.html:
• write a data contract and explain why it runs before training;
  • explain why a contract does not detect drift, and run a KS test;
  • derive a gate tolerance from measured variance, and explain why the evaluation split is part of the contract;
  • add slice gates, and handle an intentional metric trade-off through a reviewed baseline change;
  • explain paired comparisons and how alias rollback relates to image rollback;
  • read RAG thresholds as question counts, and handle embedding-model changes, cache keys and provider outages;
  • implement and justify floors and maximum-drop limits in a gate;
  • track runs and promote models with MLflow aliases;
  • build a golden set and compute hit rate, MRR and faithfulness;
  • keep LLM evaluation costs predictable with five levers;
  • present the whole pipeline in two minutes and answer follow-ups.
